profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is the Information Systems Facility at White Sands Missile Range, a large United States Army test and evaluation installation in south central New Mexico. Official US Army news coverage documents groundbreaking on August 24, 2021 for the 56,268 square foot, two story facility, built to replace a telephone and administrative network core building dating to 1962 and to consolidate networking, communications, data processing, Land Mobile Radio control, and IT support functions previously spread across multiple older buildings on the installation. The project cost approximately 70.6 million dollars in total, about 53 million dollars for construction and 17.6 million dollars for equipment, described by Army officials as the first major military construction project at White Sands Missile Range in nearly two decades, with construction projected for completion in December 2023. As a military installation facility supporting range operations, testing, and communications, no third party capacity or colocation information exists for it. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
White Sands Missile Range invested $70.6 million in a new Information Systems Facility completed in 2023, but no power consumption data is published because it is a military administrative facility, not a commercial data center.

The facility consolidates networking, communications, data processing, and IT support functions that were previously distributed across multiple buildings, including one from 1962. At 56,268 square feet across two stories, it represents the first major construction project at the range in nearly two decades. The $53 million construction cost and $17.6 million equipment budget suggest substantial infrastructure, but these figures do not translate to megawatt demand or colocation capacity.

Military installations maintain internal IT infrastructure to support their operations, but this facility does not participate in the commercial data center market and does not compete for grid power the way cloud providers or AI training operations do. No published metrics exist on its actual power draw, cooling requirements, or capacity utilization. This record documents the facility's existence and scale, but cannot inform analysis of how military computing infrastructure relates to civilian AI scaling constraints or grid demand.
